content: Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) is an extensive controlled vocabulary system designed for indexing journal articles and books in the life sciences. It is created and maintained by the United States National Library of Medicine (NLM). MeSH is utilized by the MEDLINE/PubMed article database and the NLM's catalog of book holdings. The MeSH database can be accessed and downloaded for free on the internet. However, the annual printed version of MeSH was discontinued in 2007. In the MEDLINE/PubMed system, each journal article is indexed with approximately 10 to 15 headings or subheadings. Among these, one or two are designated as major topics and are marked with an asterisk. When conducting a MEDLINE search via PubMed, entry terms are automatically translated into their corresponding MeSH descriptors. Additionally, by default, all descriptors that fall below the given term in the hierarchical structure are included in the search. Structure of MeSH The 2005 version of MeSH contains a total of 22,568 subject headings, also referred to as descriptors. Most descriptors are accompanied by a brief definition, links to related descriptors, and a list of synonyms or closely related terms, known as entry terms. These synonym lists allow MeSH to function as a thesaurus as well. Descriptors The descriptors in MeSH are organized hierarchically. A single descriptor may appear in multiple locations within the hierarchical tree. Each tree location is assigned a systematic label known as a tree number, meaning a single descriptor can have multiple tree numbers. For example, Digestive System Neoplasms has a secondary tree number of 274. Similarly, Stomach Neoplasms appears in four different locations within the hierarchy and therefore has four distinct tree numbers. These tree numbers may change as MeSH is updated, but each descriptor is also assigned a unique alphanumerical ID that remains constant. Description Most MeSH entries include a concise description. For instance, the MeSH description for diabetes type 2 provides explanatory text written by the MeSH team, based on their standard sources unless otherwise stated. These sources are typically encyclopedias and standard textbooks in the relevant subject areas. While references for specific statements in the descriptions are not provided, readers are directed to the bibliography for further information. Qualifiers In addition to the descriptor hierarchy, MeSH includes a limited number of standard qualifiers, also known as subheadings, which can be added to descriptors to refine the topic. For example, Measles is a descriptor, and epidemiology is a qualifier. The combination Measles/epidemiology refers to articles focusing on the epidemiological aspects of measles. The epidemiology qualifier can be applied to all disease descriptors. However, not all descriptor/qualifier combinations are permissible, as some may lack meaningful context. In total, there are 83 different qualifiers in MeSH. Supplements In addition to descriptors, MeSH includes approximately 139,000 Supplementary Concept Records. These records are not part of the controlled vocabulary used for indexing MEDLINE articles. Instead, they expand the thesaurus and provide links to the most closely related descriptors for use in MEDLINE searches. Many of these records describe chemical substances. MeSH has been translated into numerous languages, enabling the retrieval of documents across different languages.
